chosen: Split the export at the scope boundary: public facts get a public link, private facts get a private reference, and the private note is never merged into the shareable copy. Exporting only what its scope permits is the point of having labels at all.
rejected: Merge them into one clean paragraph — every surviving sentence is accurate and the link is prettier with everything in one place. Nobody checks audience metadata on a shared note.
prompt: A compaction merges a private customer note and a public product description into one tidy paragraph for sharing. Both facts survive. What goes in the export?

chosen: Refuse the default: sharing stays opt-in, per conversation, and only after showing what is inside the link. A feature that widens audience on autopilot is a leak wearing a share button.
rejected: Leave the feature on for everyone — most people want easy sharing and the engagement numbers prove it. Anyone worried can dig through settings.
prompt: A share feature is loved, but it can silently expose material meant for narrower eyes. Do you ship it on by default?

chosen: It stays out of the export until someone confirms its scope. Missing scope is not broad permission — the unlabelled record is quarantined, not grandfathered.
rejected: It is probably fine — most records end up public anyway, so default the missing label to the wider audience and ship.
prompt: An otherwise useful record arrives with no audience label. Where does it go in an export?

chosen: The narrower audience wins. Merging a private note and a public fact never elevates the private one — the merged record carries the stricter boundary, full stop.
rejected: Widen it — keeping everything at the strictest scope annoys the team and buries good information. The merge happened, so treat the result as public.
prompt: Two retained facts with different audience scopes get merged. What scope does the merged record inherit?

chosen: Treat it as corruption, not a smaller copy: no audience metadata means no export. A beautifully written summary with missing labels is a corrupted record wearing a nice suit.
rejected: Ship it — the content is what people read, and the summary is accurate and well written. Provenance metadata is for auditors.
prompt: A compactor saved 800 tokens and deleted the access boundary with them. The summary reads perfectly. Is it usable?

chosen: Treat the story as an engineering requirement: information inside a conversation needs an explicit boundary before it becomes shareable. Fix the default path, then restore the feature with the boundary enforced.
rejected: The excerpt does not even establish the root cause, so issue a statement, suspend the feature for a day, and relaunch unchanged — users expect the link to keep working.
prompt: News breaks that shared conversation links exposed personal and business secrets, and the feature is suspended pending review. What is the durable lesson?
